title: Event-driven and time-driven controls
blurb: Define event-driven and time-driven controls, classify PRINCE2 controls correctly and explain why every stage needs both.
question: Is a highlight report an event-driven or a time-driven control, and why does a stage need both types?

teach.body: PRINCE2 gives two types of progress control throughout a project. An event-driven control takes place when a specific event occurs. A time-driven control takes place at predefined periodic intervals. In plain English: some controls are triggered by something happening, others by the calendar.

rows.label: Examples
values: End of a stage, exception report

items: Completion of the project initiation documentation.
Organizational events that may affect the project, for example the end of the financial year.
Highlight reports produced for the project board at intervals the board defines.
Checkpoint reports on a work package at the frequency defined in the work package.

teach.body: Monitoring and reporting need a time-based rhythm, so nothing drifts unseen. Control, meaning decision-making, is event-based: the board decides at a stage end or when an exception report arrives. A stage with only events would leave the board blind between decisions; a stage with only regular reports would have nowhere for decisions to be made. PRINCE2 uses both in every stage.

teach.h: One stage, both types of control
Worked scenario: a payroll system upgrade
teach.body: At Larchfield District Council, project manager Owen Price sends a highlight report to the board every two weeks and receives weekly checkpoint reports from the supplier's team manager, Mei Lin Tan (time-driven). The council's financial year end falls mid-stage, so the board agrees to review the business case then (event-driven). When testing reveals a forecast four-week overrun, beyond stage tolerance, Owen raises an exception report straight away rather than waiting for the next highlight report.

teach.text: Classic traps: (1) Highlight and checkpoint reports are time-driven; end of stage, PID completion and exception reports are event-driven. (2) A forecast breach should not wait for the next highlight report: raising the exception report is itself an event-driven control. (3) It is not a choice of one type or the other: both are needed in every stage.

items: Event-driven: occurs when a specific event happens.
Time-driven: occurs at predefined periodic intervals.
Event examples: stage end, PID completion, exception report, financial year end.
Time examples: highlight reports, checkpoint reports.
Monitoring and reporting are time-based; control (decisions) is event-based; use both.

summary: You can now define event-driven and time-driven controls, sort PRINCE2's controls into each type and explain why a stage needs regular reports as well as event-based decision points.

A.q: Which is an example of a time-driven control?
A.why: Highlight reports are produced for the project board at predefined periodic intervals, so they are time-driven.

whyNot.0: The end of a stage is a specific event, so it is event-driven.
whyNot.2: Creating an exception report is an event-driven control.
whyNot.3: Completion of the project initiation documentation is an event-driven control.

options: A control set by the business layer
A control used by the team manager
A control applied at regular periodic intervals
A control that occurs when an event happens
A.why: An event-driven control takes place when a specific event occurs, such as a stage end.

whyNot.0: Who sets a control does not define whether it is event-driven.
whyNot.1: Team managers send time-driven checkpoint reports, so the role using a control does not make it event-driven.
whyNot.2: A control applied at regular intervals is time-driven.

A.q: Which is an example of an event-driven control?
options: The end of the financial year
A.why: Organizational events that may affect the project, such as the end of the financial year, are event-driven controls.

whyNot.0: Checkpoint reports at a set frequency are time-driven.
whyNot.1: Highlight reports at agreed intervals are time-driven.
whyNot.3: A meeting held on a fixed cycle is time-based, not triggered by an event.

B.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. Monitoring and reporting need a time-based approach, whereas control, meaning decision-making, is an [?]-based activity.
B.why: Control (decision-making) is event-based, while monitoring and reporting are time-based (manual 11.2.2).

whyNot.1: Exceptions are one kind of event, but the term contrasted with time-based is event-based.
whyNot.2: Stages provide decision points, but the term used is event-based.
whyNot.3: Plans set targets; the type of control is described as event-based.

B.q:
Which two are event-driven controls?
1. Creation of an exception report.
2. A checkpoint report.
3. The end of a stage.
4. A highlight report.
B.why: Creating an exception report (1) and the end of a stage (3) are triggered by events.

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: checkpoint reports are time-driven.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is false: highlight reports are time-driven.

B.q: Why does a stage need time-driven controls as well as event-driven ones?
options: The board makes its decisions at each regular report
Regular reports keep progress visible between decisions
Time-driven controls replace the end stage assessments
Event-driven controls stop once the PID is approved
B.why: Monitoring and reporting need a time-based rhythm so the board can see progress between event-based decision points.

whyNot.0: Decision-making is event-based, not tied to each regular report.
whyNot.2: Regular reports do not replace the end of stage decision point.
whyNot.3: Event-driven controls continue after initiation, for example at every stage end and on exception reports.

C.q: Which report is a time-driven control, and who receives it?
options: End stage report; the project board
C.why: Checkpoint reports are time-driven, sent by the team manager to the project manager at the frequency defined in the work package.

whyNot.0: The end stage report is event-driven, produced at the end of a stage.
whyNot.1: The exception report is event-driven, raised when a breach is forecast.
whyNot.3: Highlight reports go from the project manager to the project board.

C.q: A project manager forecasts a breach of stage tolerance two days after sending a highlight report. What type of control applies, and what should happen?
options: Time-driven; report it in the next highlight report
Event-driven; raise an exception report now
Time-driven; ask for an extra checkpoint report
Event-driven; wait until the end of the stage
C.why: Creating an exception report is an event-driven control: the forecast breach is escalated to the board as soon as it is identified.

whyNot.0: Waiting for the next highlight report would delay the board's decision.
whyNot.2: A checkpoint report goes to the project manager and does not escalate a stage breach.
whyNot.3: Waiting for the stage end would let the breach happen before the board can act.

C.q: Which pairing of control type and example is correct?
options: Event-driven: the completion of the PID
Time-driven: the creation of an exception report
Time-driven: the end of the financial year
C.why: Completion of the project initiation documentation is a specific event, so it is an event-driven control.

whyNot.1: Creating an exception report is event-driven.
whyNot.2: Highlight reports at set intervals are time-driven.
whyNot.3: The end of the financial year is an organizational event, so it is event-driven.

reteach.title: School reports and parents' evenings
reteach.question: How do termly reports and a call from the head teacher map onto the two controls?

blocks.h: The calendar and the phone call
blocks.body: A school sends a report every term, whatever is happening: that is time-driven. If a pupil is suddenly in serious trouble, the head teacher phones the parents that day: that is event-driven. Parents need both: regular reports to see the trend, and an immediate call when something needs a decision. PRINCE2 stages work the same way.

blocks.text: The head teacher does not wait for the end of term to report a crisis. Likewise, a forecast breach of stage tolerance does not wait for the next highlight report.

explain.body: A management control that occurs at predefined periodic intervals, such as highlight and checkpoint reports.

options: A control triggered by a forecast breach
A control at predefined periodic intervals
A control used at the end of each stage
A control agreed with the business layer
test.why: Time-driven controls occur at predefined periodic intervals.

whyNot.0: A control triggered by a forecast breach (the exception report) is event-driven.
whyNot.2: The end of a stage is an event-driven control.
whyNot.3: Who agrees a control does not make it time-driven.

explain.body: A control that occurs when a specific event happens: a stage end, PID completion, an exception report or an organizational event.

test.why: Creating an exception report is one of PRINCE2's event-driven controls.

whyNot.2: A weekly review is held on a fixed cycle, so it is time-based.

explain.body: Monitoring and reporting are time-based; control, meaning decision-making, is event-based.

test.q: Which activity is described as event-based in progress control?
test.why: Control, meaning decision-making, is an event-based activity.

whyNot.3: Recording actuals supports monitoring, which is time-based.

explain.body: Each stage uses time-driven reporting to keep progress visible and event-driven points where decisions are made.

test.q: Which statement about the two types of control is correct?
options: Both types are used in every stage
The project manager picks one type per stage
test.why: Both types of control are needed throughout the project, in every stage.

whyNot.1: Event-driven controls, such as stage ends and exception reports, continue throughout.
whyNot.2: Regular reports keep progress visible but do not replace the decision at a stage end.
whyNot.3: PRINCE2 uses both types together rather than choosing one.
